chunks.heading: 3.1.1 The system and its backgr ound
chunks.text: The system described here is often simply referred to as the ‘Quarter Remainder’ (or more literally ‘Fourth Part’) system, Si fen li 四分曆. However, the usage preferred in this book is ‘Han Quarter Remainder’ system, Han si fen li 漢四分曆, which is the term used by Li Rui in his account of this particular system, and which serves to identify it uniquely. ‘Quarter Remainder’ without qualification refers to a general type of system, of which a number of different examples are known, each of which pro- duces different results when used to calculate basic calendrical data such as the dates of solstices, equinoxes and mean conjunctions of sun and moon. The only essential point that such systems have in common is that all of them assume that the interval between winter solstices is precisely 365¼ days; additionally, all known systems of this type use the equivalence of 235 lunations to 19 solar cycles as a basis for finding when intercalary months should be inserted. As already mentioned in C hapter 1, it seems very likely that all the methods for making calculations relating to calendrical astronomy known before 104 bce were based on the ‘Quarter Remainder’ datum. The Han Quarter Remainder system was officially adopted in 85 ce, but the impulse that led to its creation was given decades earlier. I summarise here the account set out in Hou Han shu, zhi 2, translated in Chapter 5 of this book. In 32 ce, less than a decade after the beginning of Eastern Han, two high offi - cials memorialised that the Triple Concordance system, created by Liu Xin on the basis of the fundamental data fixed by the Grand Inception system in 104 bce, was predicting conjunctions of sun and moon markedly later than what was actually observed, so that the moon’s first crescent might actually be visible on the first day of the lunar month marked in the civil calendar – something which ought never to occur. But with the dynasty still engaged in re-establishing its power base, the emperor felt there was no time to attend to such matters ( Hou Han shu, zhi 2, 3025). In 62 ce, the lunar eclipse predicted by the Triple Concordance for September 8 in fact fell on the preceding day, and the attention this drew led to a year-long programme of observation, as a result of which it was eventually decided in late 69 ce that calculations of crescents and full moon dates should be made using methods based on Quarter Remainder methods. But as yet no new system The Han Quarter Remainder system Han si fen li 漢四分曆 3 was introduced, in part we are told because it was not yet possible to decide on a system origin li yuan 曆元 to replace that used by the Triple Concordance. So the dates when lunar months began and ended were calculated as before (ibid.). Finally, in 85 ce, the obvious mismatch between the heavens and the system in use – by then seen to be about ¾ day – was finally confronted. It was also noted that the predicted seasonal positions of the sun amongst the stars were five du ahead of its actual positions. Order were given to Bian Xin 編訢 and Li Fan 李梵, two experts in li, to look into the matter and make proposals for reform. On March 18 of that year, the emperor issued an edict commanding that their proposals should be put into effect, and the Triple Concordance was abandoned in favour of the Han Quarter Remainder system (Hou Han shu, zhi 2, 3026).

chunks.heading: 3.1.2 Authorship of the text
chunks.text: As noted below, the text translated here comes from the third of the monographs originally written by Sima Biao 司馬彪 (c. 240–c. 306 ce), and later incorporated in the Hou Han shu . From Sima Biao’s note at the end of this monograph, it is clear that the description of the Han Quarter Remainder system we have now was authored, or at least edited, near the end of the Eastern Han: 光和元年中， 議郎蔡邕、 郎中劉洪補續律曆志， 邕能著文， 清濁鍾律， 洪 能為筭， 述敘三光． 今考論其業， 義指博通， 術數略舉， 是以集錄為上下 篇， 放續前志， 以備一家． In the first year of the Guanghe period [178 ce], the Gentleman for Consulta- tion Cai Yong, and the Palace Gentleman Liu Hong expanded and extended the Monograph on the Pitchpipes and [Astronomical] System. Yong was able in setting out writings, and in the tuning of bells and pitchpipes, while Hong was able in calculations, and in giving an ordered account of the Three Lumi- naries. Now I have examined and evaluated their work: its ideas are broad and general, and [the details of ] numerical procedures are succinct and complete. Therefore I have collected their records into a first and second chapter, and have let them serve as a continuation of the Former Treatise, in order to make up a complete body of doctrine. (Hou Han shu, zhi 3, 3082) The ‘second chapter’ referred to is the second monograph of the Hou Han shu (translated in Chapter 5), and the ‘Former Treatise’ is the monograph on harmon- ics and the astronomical system made up of chapters 21a and 21b in the Han shu. What we have here is therefore not merely the guide to calculation methods that was presumably compiled by Bian Xin and Li Fan c. 85 ce, but also contains reflec- tions on the system by two great experts writing a century later. One of them, Liu Hong, was the creator of the Uranic Manifestation system that is the third of the systems to be translated in this book. All this goes a long way to explain some of the more discursive features of the text before us, and naturally increases its value as a historical source considerably.

chunks.heading: 3.1.3 Structur e of the system
chunks.text: This is essentially as already outlined in the account given of quarter-remainder type systems in Chapter 1. As mentioned there, a significant departure from pre- vious practice is that the Han Quarter Remainder shows clear recognition of the distinction between the celestial equator and the ecliptic.

chunks.heading: 3.1.4 Organisation of the text
chunks.text: Unlike the specification of the Triple Concordance system in the Han shu, the divi- sions of the text, though evident by their content, are not generally marked by any kind of heading. The opening section of the text is preceded by the heading li fa 曆 法 ‘Methods for [astronomical] systems’, but it is possible that this heading is really intended to label the whole text. This long section contains material of a type not found in close association with other early system descriptions. It reflects explicitly on the basis and significance of astronomical systems, and explains to some extent at least how some of the basic parameters of the system are derived from observa- tion. We can see clearly the influence of Cai Yong and Liu Hong in all this. Next comes a section in which we are given a list of 17 constants relating to the cycles of the sun and the moon; these will form the basis of future calculations. There follows a paragraph on the subject of the cycles by which lunar eclipses may be predicted, with a list of relevant constants. The next section gives the core procedures of the system, which specify how in any given year one may calculate all basic calendrical data, such as the cyclical days on which months begin, and the location of any intercalary months, together with the dates of the 24 qi which divide the interval between winter solstices into equal parts. We learn how to find the location of the sun and moon with reference to the system of 28 lodges on any date and at different times of day, and how to predict lunar eclipses. Three sections then follow on the topic of planetary motions. First, we are given the basic constants underlying the motion of each planet, then told how to use them to calculate when each planet will be in conjunction with the sun. Finally we are given for each planet a kind of ‘motion template’ dividing up the movement of the planet from one conjunction to the next into subdivisions, and specifying the daily motion of the planet for each subdivision, ending with a short note on how the data from this ‘template’ may be used to calculate from day to day where the planet is in relation to the system of 28 lodges. Next follow three tables. The first lists the months of the year, giving for each the name of the odd-numbered qi (medial qi, zhong qi 中氣) which should be found in that month if intercalations are properly carried out. The second table lists the 28 lodges, with their widths in du with reference to the celestial equator, and the third lists lodge widths with reference to the ecliptic. The first table includes ‘advance and retardation numbers’ intended to be used for conversion from one reference system to the other. The final substantive section of the text specifies how to calculate which stars will be seen on the meridian at dawn and dusk at any time of the year. This is accompanied by a tabulation of data for each of the 24 qi into which the solar cycle is divided, including the position of the sun in the lodge system, the noon shadow of a standard gnomon, the north polar distance of the sun, the duration of light and darkness, and the stars ‘centred’ on the observer’s meridian at dusk and dawn. [^1] Then the System Origin is specified, and the text closes with a historical discussion, recounting innovations in astronomical systems from High Antiquity up to the adoption of the current system, and reviewing the source materials on which the account given in this text is based.

chunks.heading: 3.1.5 Methods of calculation
chunks.text: These follow the basic principles outlined in Chapter 1. One feature that marks this system out from the other two translated in this book is the fact that it sometimes gives more than one method for achieving the same result, the second being introduced by the phrase yi shu 一術, literally ‘one method’. Once more, the impression is given that the text is not intended simply as a practical set of instructions to produce a calendar, but also has a more discursive purpose, reflecting the interests of its authors and editors.

chunks.heading: 3.1.6 T ext used
chunks.text: The following text follows the version in Hou Han shu 後漢書 (History of Eastern Han dynasty), Fan Ye 范曄 (398–445 ce), Zhonghua, Beijing: punctuated edition of 1963. Page numbers given thus ‘– 991 –’ follow that edition. Fan Ye’s main text was completed near the end of his life. However, the monographs found in the present edition were added later, using material from an earlier and now lost work by Sima Biao 司馬彪 (c. 240–c. 306 ce).[^2]

後漢書志第三 律曆下

History of the Later Han dynasty: monograph 3 Pitchpipes and [astronomical] systems: B 曆法

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
昔者聖人之作曆也， 觀琁璣之運， 三光之行， 道之發斂， 景之長短， 斗綱 (之)[所]建， 青龍所躔， 參伍以變， 錯綜其數， 而制術焉．

§1 When in former times the sages created [astronomical] systems, they watched the turning of the xuan ji, the motions of the Three Luminaries, the expansion and contraction of the Roads, the growing and shrinking of the shadow, the establishment of the Dipper mainstay, and the orbit of the Caerulean Dragon. The Three [Luminaries] and the Five [Planets] changed [their positions], and they wove together the numbers, so that they were able to make them into methods [for calculation]. This introduction underlines a radical difference of approach between its authors and Liu Xin, creator of the Triple Concordance system. Whereas he claimed to have derived the constants of his system from cosmological con- siderations, this system claims that its basic data are drawn from observation. This approach, it is claimed, represents a return to the practice of the ancient sages who created human culture in the mythical past. Some of the terms used here require a little explanation. ‘ Xuan ji’ refers to the pole star of the Han period, β Ursae minoris; the changing meanings of this term are discussed in (Cullen, Christopher and Farrer, Anne S. L. 1983); the ‘Three Luminaries’ are the sun, moon and stars; the ‘Roads’ are the paths of the sun and moon; the ‘Establishment of the Dipper’ refers to the changing directions indicated by the handle of the Dipper when first seen at dusk in successive months (see section § 3); the ‘Caerulean Dragon’, which more usually refers to one of the four creatures associated with groups of constellations correlated with the four directions here refers to the sexagenary name of the year (see sections § 5 and § 18).

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
天之動也， 一晝一夜而運過周， 星從天而西， 日違天而東． 日之所行與運周， 在 天成度， 在曆成日． 居以列宿， 終于四七， 受以甲乙， 終于六旬．

§2 In the movement of Heaven, the turning in one day and night is more than a circuit. The stars follow Heaven in moving westwards, while the sun goes against Heaven in moving eastwards. The motion of the sun and its turning round its circuit forms the du in Heaven and the days in the system. It dwells in the ordered lodges, which terminate in four sevens; it is received in the cyclical signs, which terminate in six decades. The expression ‘one day and night’ refers to a complete solar day, in which the sun returns to the same position relative to the observer. If we count from the moment of noon, this is the interval between two instants when the sun is on the meridian due south of the observer. If we count from the moment of midnight, the sun is still crossing the meridian line, but below the horizon in the north. The statement that ‘the turning in one day and night is more than a circuit’ refers to the fact that since the sun is moving from west to east against the background of the celestial sphere with the fixed stars (which turns from east to west), it follows that from one noon to the next (or one midnight to the next), since the sun has returned to the same position relative to the observe, the celestial sphere has turned a full revolution, plus the sun’s daily motion, which is in fact 1 du.

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
日月相推， 日舒月速， 當其同[所]， 謂之合朔． 舒先速後， 近一遠三， 謂之弦. 相與為衡， 分天之中， 謂之望． 以速及舒， 光盡體伏， 謂之晦． 晦朔合離， 斗建 移辰， 謂之[月]．

§3 ‘The sun and moon push one another on’. The sun is slow and the moon is fast. When they share a position, that is called a conjunction. The slow [i.e. the sun] is ahead and the fast [i.e. the moon] is behind. When they are one part near and three parts distant, that is called a crescent. When they are opposite one another, so that they divide Heaven down the middle, that is called opposition. When the fast reaches the slow, so that its bril - liance is exhausted and its form is hidden, that is called darkening [as on the last day of a lunar month]. When darkening and conjunction have joined and separated, and the Dipper Establishment shifts by a sign, that is called a month. The first sentence refers to the Book of Change, which contains the following passage:

日往則月來， 月往則日來， 日月相推而明生焉. 《易經》《繫辭下》

The sun departs and the moon comes, the moon departs and the sun comes, the sun and moon push one another on, and brilliance is produced by them. (Zhou yi 周易, 8, 169A in Shi san jing zhu shu edn. [Ruan Yuan 阮元 1973 reprint of original of 1815])

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
日月之(術)[行]， 則有冬有夏 ；冬夏之閒， 則有春有秋． 是故日行北陸謂之 冬， 西陸謂之春， 南陸謂之夏， 東陸謂之秋． 日道發南， 去極彌遠， 其景彌長, 遠長乃極， 冬乃至焉． 日道斂北， 去極彌近， 其景彌短， 近短乃極， 夏乃至焉. 二至之中， 道齊景正， 春秋分焉．

§4 Through the motion of the sun and moon, there is winter and there is sum - mer. Between winter and summer, there is spring and there is autumn. Thus when the sun moves through the northern regions, that is called winter; through the western regions it is called spring; through the southern regions it is called summer, and through the eastern regions it is called autumn. When the sun’s path extends out southwards, it goes ever further from the pole, and the shadow becomes ever longer, and when distance and length reach their extreme, then winter culminates there. When the sun’s path draws in towards the north, it goes ever closer to the pole, and the shadow is ever shorter, and when nearness and shortness reach their extreme, then summer culminates there. Between the two extremes [sc. ‘solstices’], the path is even and the shadow is true, and spring and autumn are divided there. The ‘regions’ through which the sun moves are the four quarters of the heavenly sphere corresponding to its position during the four seasons. The labelling as ‘north’ and so forth in the third sentence is conventional rather than directional. The meaning becomes literal in the rest of the section, where it is stated that when the sun is at its northernmost the season is summer, and when it is at its southernmost the seasons is winter.

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
日周于天， 一寒一暑， 四時備成， 萬物畢改， 攝提遷次， 青龍移辰， 謂之歲．歲 首至也， 月首朔也． 至朔同日謂之章， 同在日首謂之蔀， 蔀終六旬謂之紀，歲 朔又復謂之元． 是故日以實之， 月以閏之， 時以分之，歲以周之， 章以明之， 蔀以部之， 紀以記之， 元以原之． 然後雖有變化萬殊， 贏朒無方， 莫不結系于 此而稟正焉．

§5 The sun circuits round Heaven: there is one cold and one heat, the four seasons are all complete, the myriad creatures are all changed, the sheti [i.e. the 12 cyclical characters referring to years] shift their station, and the Cae - rulean Dragon [i.e. the sexagenary name of the year] moves its mark-point. This is called a sui. The head of the sui is the [winter] solstice, and the head of the yue is the conjunction. When the solstice and the conjunction fall on the same day, that is called a Rule [Head].When this takes place at the head of a day [i.e. midnight], this is called an Obscuration [Head]. When an Obscuration has terminated the six decades, that is called an Era [Head]. When the sui and the conjunction both return, that is called an Origin [Head]. So for the day one fills it, for the yue one intercalates it, for the season one divides it, for the sui one circuits it, for the Rule one illuminates it, for the Obscuration one sections it, for the Era one records it, and for the Origin one traces it to the source. Only when this is done, then even if there are transformations and a myriad variations, and expansions and contraction without limitation, then there is nothing that is not bound up with these and are endowed and rectified by them. I have deliberately refrained from providing a translation of the term ‘ sui’ 歲 and ‘yue’ 月 in this section, which illustrates rather well the double reference involved in the use of these words, as was discussed in Chapt er 1. In its first occurrence ‘sui’ evidently refers to the calendrical unit that we may call the civil year, normally consisting of 12 whole months of either 29 or 30 whole days each. However, we are next told that the ‘sui’ starts at winter solstice – which is by no means always the case for the civil year, so that the reference is clearly to what I have chosen to call the ‘solar cycle’. As already explained, in the period covered by this book it was assumed that the winter solstice was at a fixed position relative to the stars, so that (in modern terms) the tropical and sidereal years were equal. Similar considerations apply to the choice between the translations ‘month’ and ‘lunation’ for yue 月. The other periods mentioned are explained below: see section § 18. Their durations are: Rule: 19 years Obscuration: 76 years Era: 1520 years Origin: 4560 years The sentence beginning ‘So for the day one fills it . . .’ cont ains a number of plays on words, sometimes involving assonance.

This is called a sui. The head of the sui is the [winter] solstice, and the head of the yue is the conjunction. When the solstice and the conjunction fall on the same day, that is called a Rule [Head].When this takes place at the head of a day [i.e. midnight], this is called an Obscuration [Head]. When an Obscuration has terminated the six decades, that is called an Era [Head]. When the sui and the conjunction both return, that is called an Origin [Head]. So for the day one fills it, for the yue one intercalates it, for the season one divides it, for the sui one circuits it, for the Rule one illuminates it, for the Obscuration one sections it, for the Era one records it, and for the Origin one traces it to the source. Only when this is done, then even if there are transformations and a myriad variations, and expansions and contraction without limitation, then there is nothing that is not bound up with these and are endowed and rectified by them. I have deliberately refrained from providing a translation of the term ‘ sui’ 歲 and ‘yue’ 月 in this section, which illustrates rather well the double reference involved in the use of these words, as was discussed in Chapt er 1. In its first occurrence ‘sui’ evidently refers to the calendrical unit that we may call the civil year, normally consisting of 12 whole months of either 29 or 30 whole days each. However, we are next told that the ‘sui’ starts at winter solstice – which is by no means always the case for the civil year, so that the reference is clearly to what I have chosen to call the ‘solar cycle’. As already explained, in the period covered by this book it was assumed that the winter solstice was at a fixed position relative to the stars, so that (in modern terms) the tropical and sidereal years were equal. Similar considerations apply to the choice between the translations ‘month’ and ‘lunation’ for yue 月. The other periods mentioned are explained below: see section § 18. Their durations are: Rule: 19 years Obscuration: 76 years Era: 1520 years Origin: 4560 years The sentence beginning ‘So for the day one fills it . . .’ cont ains a number of plays on words, sometimes involving assonance.

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
極建其中， 道營于外， 琁衡追日， 以察[發]斂， 光道生焉． 孔壺為漏， 浮箭為 刻， 下漏數刻， 以考中星， 昏明生焉．

§6 The pole is established in the centre, and the Roads are constructed outside. The Xuan and Heng pursue the sun, 3 and by investigating its outwards and inwards [displacement], the Brilliant Road is created. The perforated vessel performs its dripping, and the floating arrow makes its divisions. One lets the drips go down and counts the divisions, and by examining the centred stars, dusk and dawn are created. Here and in the next section, ‘Brilliant Road’ is an alternative name for the ecliptic, elsewhere referred to as huang dao 黃道 ‘The Yellow Road’. The ‘perforated ves - sel’ is a simple outflow clepsydra, with the aid of which we are to time the passage of a standard repertoire of stars as they cross the meridian, and thus are ‘centred’ zhong 中 due south. From such observations, it is possible to predict which stars should cross the meridian near dawn and dusk at any given time of the year: see section 3.2.9. [^4]

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
日有光道， 月有九行， 九行出入而交生焉． 朔會望衡， 鄰於所交， 虧薄生焉． 月 有晦朔， 星有合見， 月有弦望， 星有留逆， 其歸一也， 步術生焉．

§7 The sun has its Brilliant Road, and the Moon has its Nine Ways. The Nine Ways go out and in, and the Nodes are produced thereby. When the meeting at conjunction and the diametricality at opposition are near to the position of the Nodes, then waning and concealment [sc. solar or lunar eclipses] are produced thereby. The Moon has its darkening and conjunction; stars [sc. plan- ets] have their conjunction and appearance; the Moon has its crescent and full, stars [sc. planets] have their stationary points and retrogradation. They all go back to a single [basis], and predictive methods are produced thereby. In this section, the jiu dao 九道 ‘Nine Roads’ clearly refer to the moon, whereas in the Triple Concordance they appeared to refer to the sun. The topic of the nodes (the points where the moon’s path crosses the ecliptic) does not recur later in this text. See however the discussion in relation to Jia Kui’s work c. 100 ce, in the document collection of Cai Yong and Liu Hong elsewhere in the Hou Han shu, translated later in this book in Chapt er 5.

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
金、水承陽， 先後日下， 速則先日， 遲而後留， 留而後逆， 逆與日違， 違而後速, 速與日競， 競又先日， 遲速順逆， 晨夕生焉． 日、月、五緯各有終原， 而七元生 焉． 見伏有日， 留行有度， 而率數生焉． 參差齊之， 多少均之， 會終生焉．

§8 Metal [Mercury] and Water [Venus] sustain Yang, and precede and follow beneath the sun. When they are fast they precede the sun, and when they are slow they begin to lag. When they lag they retrograde, and retrograding they transgress against the sun. After retrograding they speed up, and speeding up they go neck and neck with the sun, and after going neck and neck they precede the sun again. Slowing and speeding up, direct and retrograde motion, dawn and dusk [visibility] are thereby produced. The Sun, Moon and Five Wefts [sc. planets] each have their terminations and starting points, and the Seven Origins are thereby produced. Appearance and disappearance [of plan- ets] have their days, stationary points and movement have their degrees, and the numerical proportions are thereby produced. That which not uniform one evens out; that which is greater or lesser one equalises, and compatibility and completion is produced thereby. The reference in the last sentence is apparently to the ways in which observational data are evaluated to produce constants for the mean movements of planets, as specified later in this text.

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
引而伸之， 觸而長之， 探賾索隱， 鉤深致遠， 無幽辟潛伏， 而不以其精者 然.故陰陽有分， 寒暑有節， 天地貞觀， 日月貞明．

§9 So [as in the words of the Book of Change] one ‘draws forth the general [from the particular], and on coming across some [category] 5 one expands it’; ‘one seeks out the profound and draws forth the obscure, hooks out the deep and brings near the distant’, so that there is nothing that is recondite or hidden, whatever its subtlety may be. So Yin and Yang have their division, cold and heat have their regularities, ‘Heaven and Earth are made authentically manifest, and the Sun and Moon are made authentically brilliant.’

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
若夫祐術開業， 淳燿天光， 重黎其上也． [一]承聖帝之命若昊天， 典曆象三 辰， 以授民事， 立閏定時， 以成歲功， 羲和其隆也． [二]取象金火， 革命創制， 治曆明時， 應天順民， 湯、武其盛也． [三]及王德之衰也， 無道之君亂之於 上， 頑愚之史失之於下． 夏后之時， 羲和淫湎， 廢時亂日， 胤乃征之． 紂作淫 虐， 喪其甲子， 武王誅之． 夫能貞而明之者， 其興也勃焉；回 而敗之者， 其亡也忽焉． 巍巍乎若道天地之綱紀， 帝王之壯事， 是以聖人寶 焉， 君子勤之．

§10 It was Chongli [= Zhuanxu 顓頊, grandson of the Yellow Emperor] who was the first to bestow his august patronage on these methods, inaugurate this heritage and make the Heavenly brilliance pure and radiant. It was Xi and He who played a glorious part in taking up the Sage Lord’s command to accord with august Heaven, to set up canons, sequences and counterparts for the Three Markers [the sun, moon and stars], in order to grant their tasks to the people, setting up intercalations to correct the seasons, and thus completing the year’s accomplishments. It was [King] Tang and [King] Wu who achieved complete success in taking Metal and Fire as their counterparts,[^6] changing the Mandate and creating ordinances, regulating the calendar and making clear the seasons, being responsive to Heaven and making the people amenable. But then it came to the time of decay of kingly virtue, when above there was disorder by rulers who lacked the Way, and below stupid Clerks lost [the thread]. In the time of Xiahou [sc. the Xia dynasty], the Xi and He officials were debauched by wine, abandoning the seasons and disordering the days, whereupon [the marquis of] Yin proceeded against them. Tchou 7 [last Ruler of the Shang dynasty] was debauched and tyran - nous, abandoning the sexagenary sequence of days, and King Wu punished him. For one who is able to clarify these matters authentically, their rise is swift; for those who turn back and do harm, their fall is sudden. How great it is, like telling of the sustaining cords of Heaven and Earth, and the solid work of Lords and Kings. Thus the Sage treasures these things, and the Gentlemen exerts his diligence therein. The basis element of this story, which takes us from mythical rulers of High Antiquity down to the undoubtedly historical early kings of the Zhou dynasty c. 1 046 bce, are repeated in a number of accounts such as the present one. See also the material from the Han shu translated in Chap ter 5. The point being made is that good and effective rulers ensure that effective astronomical systems are adopted.

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
夫曆有聖人之德六焉：以本氣者尚其體， 以綜數者尚其文， 以考類者尚其 象， 以作事者尚其時， 以占往者尚其源， 以知來者尚其流．

§11 There are six ways in which the virtue of the Sage is contained in an [astronomical] system. By taking the qi as basic, it exalts the form [of Heaven]. By threading together the numbers, it exalts the patterns [of Heaven]. By examining the categories, it exalts the counterparts [of Heaven]. By carrying out its task, it exalts the seasons [of Heaven]. By divining from what is past, it exalts the source, [which is Heaven]. By knowing what is to come, it exalts the onwards movement [of Heaven].

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
大業載之， 吉凶生焉， 是以君子將有興焉， 咨焉而以從事， 受命而莫之 違也． 若夫用天因地， 揆時施教， 頒諸明堂， 以為民極者， 莫大乎月令. 帝王之大司備矣， 天下之能事畢矣． 過此而往， 羣忌苟禁， 君子未之或

知也． §12 The Great Task sustains it, and good and evil fortune come forth from it. Therefore, when the gentleman is to undertake some new matter, he looks into it in order to be able to carry on his work; he accepts the Mandate and does not go against it. For making use of Heaven and basing oneself upon Earth, for judging the seasons and proclaiming the teaching, so that it can be told forth in the Hall of Holiness, to be the people’s Ultimate, nothing is greater than the Monthly Ordinances. 8 [In them] the great charges of emperors and kings are complete, and all the most demanding affairs of the Empire are accomplished. If one goes outside these [limits], fears and confusions abound intolerably and no gentleman has ever known of it.

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
斗之二十一度， 去極至遠也， 日在焉而冬至， 羣物於是乎生． 故律首黃鍾， 曆 始冬至， 月先建子， 時平夜半．

§13 The twenty-first du of Dipper is [the position of the Sun when it is at] the maximum distance from the pole. When the sun is situated there it is the winter solstice: that is the time when all things begin to be produced. Thus the head of the pitch-pipes is Yellow Bell, [astronomical] systems begin from winter solstice, the months give precedence to the establishment zi [the 11th month in the ‘Xia’ count used today, the first Celestial month], and time of day is made even with midnight. The Triple Concordance system placed the sun at the start of the lodge Ox at the winter solstice. This would have corresponded closely to reality around 450 bce, when the two bright stars of Ox, β and α Capricorni, would have been close to longitude 270°, and hence on the winter solsticial colure. It is however important to realise that the winter solstice position of the sun is not directly observable by the naked eye, but can only be deduced indirectly, by (for instance) observing the stars crossing the meridian at midnight at the summer solstice, an observation which is crucially dependent on accurate time measurement. It would therefore be unsafe to assume that the use of Ox as a winter solstice marker reflects actual observation in the mid-fifth-century bce. By around 50 ce precession had changed the longitude of these stars to about 277°, since the winter solstice position had shifted westwards to the preceding lodge, Dipper. Dipper was (according to the Han Quarter Remainder system) 26¼ du in width, so that the position given here was not a bad estimate, since it implied that the winter solstice was about 5 du (close to 5º) to the west of the start of Ox, and the actual distance was similar, at about 7 du. The fact that that Liu Xin still used the position at the start of Ox when he constructed the Triple Concordance suggests that this datum was accepted on the basis of tradition rather than observation. In 92 ce Jia Kui noted that different systems had used different winter solstice positions:

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
古黃帝、夏、殷、周、魯冬至日在建星， 建星即今斗星也．

At the winter solstice of the ancient Yellow Emperor, Xia, Yin, Zhou and Lu systems,[^9] the sun is at the Establishment Star, and the Establishment Star is our modern Dipper Star. (Hou Han shu, zhi 2, 3027) See the continuation of the discussion by Jia Kui in Chapt er 5.

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
當漢高皇帝受命四十有五歲， 陽在上章， 陰在執徐， 冬十有一月甲子夜半朔 旦冬至， 日月閏積之數皆自此始， 立元正朔， 謂之漢曆． 又上兩元， 而月食五 星之元， 並發端焉．

§14 In the forty-fifth year after the High Sovereign Emperor of Han received the mandate, when the Yang was at shangzhang [the seventh of its 10 posi- tions], and the Yin was at zhixu [its fifth position out of 12], in winter, the eleventh month, day jiazi.1, at midnight, the moment of conjunction [occurred at the same time as] the winter solstice. The reckonings of the sun, moon and accumulation of intercalations starts from this point. It establishes the origin and standardises the conjunction. This is called the Han System. Going back a further two Origins, then that is the origin for lunar eclipses and the five planets, which all start from this point. The instant of System Origin here defined is December 25, 162 bce, at midnight local time at Luoyang (longitude 112° 37.8’ E), Julian Day Number 1,662,610.18750. Two Origins back takes us to Luoyang midnight beginning December 25, 9281 bce, Julian Day Number −1,668,469.81250. Shangzhang is the seventh of 10 possible positions for Yang, corresponding to the stem geng 庚, while zhixu corresponds to the seventh of 12 possible Yin positions, corresponding to the branch chen 辰. chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
曆數之生也， 乃立儀、表， 以校日景． 景長則日遠， 天度之端也． 日發其 端,周而為歲， 然其景不復， 四周千四百六十一日， 而景復初， 是則日行之終． 以周除日， 得三百六十五四分度之一， 為歲之日數． 日日行一度， 亦為天度．

§15 In the process of producing the numbers of the astronomical system, one sets up [armillary] instruments and gnomons,[^10] in order to compare the solar shadows. When the shadow is longest the sun is most distant; this is the starting point for the degrees of heaven. The sun sets out from that starting point, and makes a sui when it has circuited. However the shadow does not return: the shadow returns to its starting point after four circuits, 1461 days, and so this represents the termination of the sun’s motion. Casting out circuits from the days, one obtains 365 and ¼, which is the number of days in a sui. The sun moves one du in a day, so [this figure] is also the du in [a circuit of] the heavens. ‘Sui’ here clearly means ‘solar cycle’ rather than ‘year’.

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
察日月俱發度端， 日行十九周， 月行 二百五十四周， 復會于端， 是則月行之終也． 以日周除月周， 得一歲周天 之數． 以日一周減之， 餘十二十九分之七， 則月行過周及日行之數也， 為一 歲之月． 以除一歲日， 為一月之數． 月之餘分積滿其法， 得一月， 月成則其

歲[大]． §16 If one examines the sun and moon as together they leave the starting point for du, when the sun has travelled 19 circuits, and the moon has travelled 254 circuits, they meet once more at the starting point. When this [happens], it is the termination of lunar motion. Casting out solar circuits from lunar circuits, one obtains the number of [lunar] circuits in a solar cycle. Casting out one solar circuit from that leaves a remainder of 12 7/19 which is the number of times the moon moves through more than a circuit and meets the sun, which is the number of lunations in a solar cycle. If [by that quan- tity] one casts out from the days in a solar cycle, that makes the number [of days in] a lunation. When the remainder parts of lunations [in a solar cycle] fill the factor, one gets a month, and when a month is formed the year is a large one [i.e. with an intercalary month]. This section describes the astronomical basis and implications of the Rule Cycle, which will be referred to in section § 18, and is also used in the other two systems translated in this book. Since the moon will actually move past the sun 254 − 19 = 235 times, the implication is that 19 solar cycles are precisely equal in duration to 235 lunations. Since 235 = 19 in 12 + 7, we must insert seven intercalary lunar months in the course of 19 civil years in order to maintain correspondence between the months and the seasons. 254/19 = 13 + 7⁄19, the number of lunar circuits of heaven in a solar cycle. Thus 12 + 7⁄19 is the number of lunations in a solar cycle. The number of days in a lunation is: (365 ¼) (1 2 + 7⁄19) = 29 499⁄940 days The reference to ‘filling the factor’ works as follows: One solar cycle = 12 + 7⁄19 lunations Two solar cycles = 24 + 14⁄19 lunations Three solar cycles = 36 + 21⁄19 lunations = 36 + 1 + 2⁄19 lunations Thus the 3rd civil year must contain an extra month in order to keep in step with the solar cycle, since the fractional parts of a month have built up to more that 19, which is ‘the factor’, more specifically the ‘Rule Factor’; see section § 24.

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
月(大)四時推移， 故置十二中以定月位． 有朔而無中者為閏月． 中之始(日) [曰]節， 與中為二十四氣． 以除一歲日， 為一氣之日數也． 其分積而成日為 沒 ，并歲氣之分， 如法為一歲沒． 沒分于終中， 中終于冬至， 冬至之分積如其 法得一日， 四歲而終．

§17 In the case of months, the four seasons shift [in relation to them], and so one sets out the 12 Medial [Qi] in order to fix the places of the months. When a conjunction occurs without a Medial [Qi], that makes an intercalary month. The start of a Medial [Qi] is called a Nodal [Qi], and together with the Medials these make the 24 qi. If by this one casts out from the days of one year, that makes the number of days in one qi. If the fractions accu- mulate to complete one day, that makes an Extinction. If one adds up the fractions of the qi of a year, then if these accord with their factor, that makes one Year Extinction. The Extinction fractions are divided amongst the terminating Medials; the Medials are terminated at the winter solstice. When the fractions at the winter solstice accumulate to accord with their factor, one gets one day, and this is concluded after four years. We have already met the ‘no medial qi’ rule for intercalation in the Triple Concor- dance system. The number of days in one Qi is: (365 ¼) /2 4 = 15 7⁄32 The meaning and application of the term ‘Extinction’ is made clear in detail in

chunks.heading: 3.2.1 Methods for [astronomical] systems
chunks.text:
月分成閏， 閏七而盡， 其歲十九， 名之曰章． 章首分盡， 四之俱終， 名之曰蔀. 以一歲日乘之， 為蔀之日數也． 以甲子命之， 二十而復其初， 是以二十蔀為 紀 ．紀歲青龍未終， 三終歲後復青龍為元．

§18 The fractions of a lunation complete an intercalation, and these intercalations are exhausted after seven. The years are 19, which is called a Rule. When the fractions at the head of a Rule are exhausted, and the fours are all terminated, this is called an Obscuration. If one multiplies by the days of one year, this is the number of days of an Obscuration. If one counts off by the sexagenary day name [lit. ‘the jiazi’], it returns to the beginning [after] 20. So 20 Obscurations make an Era. In the years of an Era the Caerulean Dragon is not yet concluded, so after three completions of [this number of] years one returns to the Caerulean Dragon, making an Origin. In the first two sentences, we are reminded that seven intercalations take place in a Rule cycle of 19 years. Since however 19 solar cycles are 365¼ days × 19 = 6939¾ days we shall have to finish four Rules – an Obscuration, 76 years – before we have a whole number of days, and winter solstice and conjunction once more coincide at midnight. Since an Obscuration contains 27,759 days, we shall need 20 Obscurations – an Era, 1520 years – before the days elapsed are a multiple of 60 and the sexagenary day name repeats. But since 1520 is not a multiple of 60, we need three Eras – an Origin, 4560 years – before the sexagenary year number returns to system origin conditions. This section makes it plain that the term ‘Caerulean Dragon’ is being used as a name for the sexagenary year-name. This usage can be traced back to the Huai nan zi book in the second century bce: see (Huai nan hong lie ji jie 3, 125–126) and (Major, John S., with an appendix by Christopher Cullen 1993: 133–135).

§19 Origin Factor: 4560. 4560 = 76 × 60, so the sexagenary name of the year repeats after Origin Factor years. 4560 × 365¼ = 1,665,540 = 27,759 × 60, so the sexagenary day name repeats after Origin Factor solar cycles, which is a whole number of days. 4560 × 235/19 = 56,400, so this period also contains a whole number of luna - tions, ensuring that Origin Factor years after System Origin, winter solstice and conjunction once more coincide at midnight.

§26 Circuits of Heaven: 1461. 1461 = 365¼ × 4 This is the number of days in a solar cycle at a scale of Day Factor [4] – or alterna- tively the number of days in 4 solar cycles, which is a whole number. Since an Obscuration is 4 × 19 = 76 years, which contain 4 × 235 = 940 lunations, an Obscuration contains 19 × 1461 days. Thus the mean length of a lunation is 19 × 1461/940 days = 29 499⁄940 days. Each (1/19) of a month is clearly 1461/940 days, so multiplying by Circuits of Heaven [1461] converts months at a scale of 19 to days at a scale of 940.

chunks.heading: 3.2.3 [Lunar eclipse constants]
chunks.text:
月食數之生也， 乃記月食之既者． 率二十三食而復既， 其月(食)百三十五， 率 之相除， 得五(百)[月]二十三之二十而一食． 以除一歲之月， 得歲有再食五 百一十三分之五十[五]也． 分終其法， 因以與蔀相約， 得四與二十七， 互之， 會二千五十二， 二十而與元會．

§36 In producing the numbers for lunar eclipses, one records instances where the lunar eclipse is total. The rate is that after 23 eclipses totality returns, and the months are 135. If the rates are cast out, one gets one eclipse per

5 20/23 months. If by that one casts out from the months of a year, one finds that in a year there are 2 55/513 eclipses. When the fractions terminate their factor, and one makes this compatible with the Obscuration, one gets 4 and 27. Changing it round, the Concidence [occurs at] 2052, and in 20 of these there is Coincidence with the Origin. This is how the figures work out: The notion of a cycle of 23 lunar eclipses in 135 months predates the Eastern Han. The cycle begins with a lunar eclipse at the full moon of the first month of the cycle, and the last eclipse falls at the full moon of the 131st month. The next lunar eclipse is at full moon of the first month of the next 135- month cycle. 135/23 = 5 + 20/23, so this is the mean number of months between eclipses – although actual eclipses must of course be separated by whole numbers of months, since they must fall at full moon. The mean number of months in a civil year taken over a complete Rule of 19 years is 235/19. So the mean number of eclipses per year is given by: (235/19) / (135/23) = (235 × 23) / (19 × 135) Dividing top and bottom by 5, we obtain: (47 × 23) / (19 × 27) = 1081/513 = 2 + 55/513 which is the mean number of eclipses in one year. Now an Obscuration is 4 × 19 = 76 years So in an Obscuration, the number of eclipses is: (4 × 19) × (47 × 23) / (19 × 27) = (4 × 47 × 23) / 27 = 4324/27 So in 27 Obscurations there are 4324 eclipses. Note that since there are 940 months in an Obscuration, 27 Obscurations contains: 27 × 940/135 = 188 cycles of 135 months, each with 23 eclipses in the same pattern. 27 Obscurations is 27 × 76 = 27 × 4 × 19 = 2052 years. This is an Obscura - tion Coincidence. However 2052 mod 60 = 12, so the sexagenary year number of successive Obscuration Coincidences will shift by this amount. Taking 5 Obscuration Coincidences would bring return of the sexagenary year number, but the result would not yet be a multiple of the Origin Factor (4560). This results when we take 4 × 5 = 20 Obscuration Coincidences since: 20 × 2052 = 41,040 = 9 × 4560 At the interval of 41,040 years we therefore have a repetition of lunar eclipse at full moon of the first Celestial month, commencing with coincidence of conjunction, midnight and winter solstice with repetition of sexagenary day name and sexagenary year-name. This interval is Origin Coincidence.

chunks.heading: 3.2.4 [Pr ocedures for sun and moon]
chunks.text:
推入蔀術曰 以元法除去上元， 其餘以紀法除之， 所得數從天紀， 筭外則所入紀也． 不滿 紀法者， 入紀年數也． 以蔀法除之， 所得數從甲子蔀起, 筭外, [所入蔀也 不滿蔀法者入蔀年數也各以]所入(紀)[蔀] 歲名命之， 筭上， 即所求年太歲

所在． Obscuration: §43 Cast out Origin Factor [4560] from accumulated years from Grand Origin. Cast out Era Factor [1520] from the remainder. Number from the Heaven Era by how many you obtain, then outside the count is the Era you are entering. As for what does not amount to an Era Factor [1520], it is the number of years entered into the Era. Cast out Obscuration Factor [76] from it. Number from the jiazi.1 Obscuration by how many you obtain, then outside your count, [that is the Obscuration which is being entered. As for what does not amount to an Obscuration Factor [76], that is the number of years into the Obscuration. In each case] label that by the year-name of the (Era) [Obscuration] into which one had entered, then above the count [i.e. the next [position in sequence after the last one counted], that is where the Great Year [= year-name] is in the year sought. The text seems slightly garbled near the end though it is clear what is intended. The proposed emendation by the editors deals with the problem; its length sug - gests that a scribe may have skipped a column of characters. The further emendation of ‘Era’ to ‘Obscuration’ is also helpful. The aim of this section is to find the sexagenary number (year-name) of the year now beginning. We do this by finding the sexagenary number of the first year of the current Obscuration, and then counting forward. The requisite data are provided in Table 3.1. First we cast out whole Origins, since all relevant conditions repeat in an Origin. Since an Origin is three Eras, we then establish which of the three Eras of the current Origin we are in. That tells us which of the three main columns (in the modern format – rows in the original) we should be using. The columns are named after Heaven, Earth and Man – Celestial, Terrestrial and Anthropic. Each column has in its first row the sexagenary number of its first year. Each column has 20 rows, containing the sexagenary numbers of the first year of each of the 20 Obscurations that make up the relevant Era. The rows are numbered 1 to 20 at the extreme left, just after the fourth column in which we are given the sexagenary number of the day on which the Obscurations in each row begin. All Obscurations on the same row share the same initial day name, since they are separate by a whole Era of 1520 years, and: 1520 × 365.25 = 555,180 = 9253 × 60 To judge from the text, it seems that the sexagenary name of the initial day is used as a name for each row, rather than the actual number of the row. To find which row we are in, it is necessary to cast out whole Obscurations from the remainder after casting out Eras. The number of complete Obscurations tells us how many rows to count downwards – no complete Obscurations leaves us at the first row, and 19 (the maximum) takes us down to the 20th and final row. The remainder after casting out whole Obscurations is the number of complete years into the current Obscuration. If it is zero, then we stay at the year-name given in the table. The maximum remainder of 75 will increase the tabulated number by 75 mod 60 = 15, one less than the next tabulated number.

chunks.text:
推月食所入蔀會年: 以元會除去上元， 其餘以蔀會除之， 所得以(七)[二]十(二)[七]乘之， 滿 六十除去之， 餘以二十除所得數， 從天紀， 筭(之起)外， 所(以)入紀， 不滿二 十者， 數從甲子蔀起， 筭外， 所入蔀會也． 其初不滿蔀會者， 入蔀會年數也， 各 以(不)[所]入紀歲名命之， 筭上， 即所求年(蔀)[太歲所在]．

eclipse: §44 From the distance from High Origin cast out Origin Coincidence [41,040]. From the remainder, cast out Obscuration Coincidence [2052], and multiply what you obtain by 27. Cast out what fills 60, and from the number you obtain cast out 20. Start from the Heaven Era, and outside the exhausted count, that is the Era entered. With what does not fill 20, count starting from the jiazi.1 Obscuration, and outside the count, that is the Obscuration entered. What initially did not fill Obscuration Coincidence is the number of years by which the Obscuration Coincidence is entered. In each case count off from the year name of the Era entered, and above the count, that is where the Great Year is in the year sought. Casting out Origin Coincidences eliminates repetition of the initial conditions of the system, including lunar eclipses. Casting out Obscuration Coincidences eliminates repetition of initial conditions, except that each Obscuration Coincidence that passes will shift the year-name by a fixed amount, given by: 2052 mod 60 = 12 Instead of following this route directly, however, the text prefers to use the table provided, which requires us to use the normal year cycles (Origin, Era, Obscura- tion) rather than the special eclipse cycles (Origin Coincidence, Obscuration Coincidence). Each Obscuration Coincidence [2052] contains 27 Obscurations [76], so after multiplying whole numbers of Obscuration Coincidences by 27 we have the whole number of Obscurations elapsed. Since 20 Obscurations [76] make an Era [1520], 3 of which make an Origin, casting out groups of 60 Obscurations as instructed casts out Origins, thus eliminating repetition of initial conditions. We then cast out Eras by casting out groups of 20 Obscurations from the Remain- der. The number of whole Eras left after casting out Origins can only be zero, one or two. Zero places us in the Celestial Column in the table below, one in the Terrestrial column, and 2 in the Anthropic column, as explained in the previ - ous section. What is left from all this is the number of whole Obscurations so far in the cur - rent Era, and using this number we count down from the first row to find the year-name of the first year of the current Obscuration – which is of course the year-name of the first year of the current Obscuration Coincidence. The final step is to take the number of years into the current Obscuration Coin - cidence, and use that to count off from the year-name of the first year of the Obscuration Coincidence, which we have just found. Although the text does not specify, we will clearly start by casting out multiples of 60.

[TABLE_3_1] §45 [T able of year-names]

[TABLE_3_2] How does this table work? We begin in the year designated gengchen.17, whose first day is jiazi.1. This is the head of an Origin [4560], an Era [1520], an Obscuration [76] and a Rule [19]. Since 1520 = 25 × 60 + 20, then one Era later the year-name will have increased by 20, to become gengzi.37; another Era later it will be gengshen.57. The next Era will start again in year gengchen.17. However, 1520 × 365.25 = 7980 = 133 × 60. So a whole number of sexagenary day cycles has elapsed from the start of one Era to the next, and the day name of the first day of the Rule that begins the first Obscuration of each new Era in the sequence is unchanged. If however we begin from the original starting point, but go forward only one Obscuration, 76 years, to the start of the second of the 20 Obscurations that make up the initial Era, then since 76 = 60 + 16, the year-name must increase by 16 from gengchen.17 to bingshen.33. Also, since 76 × 365.25 = 462 × 60 + 39, the day name changes from jiazi.1 to guimao.40. To sum up: Each horizontal row has in its first three places the year-names of the starts of three successive Eras, making up an Origin. The fourth position gives the day name of the start of the Obscuration with which each set of three Eras begins. Each row down the table represents conditions one Obscuration later than the row above.

chunks.heading: 3.2.4 [Pr ocedures for sun and moon]
chunks.text:
推天正術， 置入蔀年減一， 以章月乘之， 滿章法得一， 名為積月， 不滿為閏餘， 十二以上, 其歲有閏．

§46 Set out the years into the Obscuration and subtract one. Multiply by Rule Months [235]. Count one for each Rule Factor [19] filled. Call this Accu- mulated Months. The remainder is the Intercalation Remainder. If it is 12 or more, this year has an intercalation. This section and the next aim to predict the sexagenary day name of the first day of the first month of the current year according to the Celestial count. We start from the beginning of the current Obscuration, at which we are guaranteed that midnight, conjunction beginning the first Celestial month and winter solstice coin- cide. We already know (from Proc. 3.3) the sexagenary day name with which the Obscuration begins. Here we aim to find how many whole months have elapsed since the start of the Obscuration, and to predict whether the current civil year has an intercalary month or not. The first procedure deals with the fact that ‘years into the obscuration’ 入 蔀 年 means the ordinal number of year in the Obscuration. Since we want the number of years from the start of the Obscuration to the start of the current year, we have to subtract one from this number. Then we use the fact that 235 months are exactly equivalent to 19 years to find how many whole months have elapsed since the start of the Obscuration. The remainder will be a fraction of a month at a scale of Rule Factor [19]. This is the Intercalation Remainder, and may be taken as the pending fraction of a new intercalary month representing the amount by which the start of the new year is in advance of its ideal date, which should coincide with winter solstice. Now since 235/19 is 12 + 7/19, it is clear that by the end of the year we are now starting the Intercalation Remainder will have increased by 7. So if at the start of the current year this Remainder is 12 or more, the Remainder will at least have reached 19 by the end of the year, calling for a delay of a whole month before the next year starts – which requires an intercalary month to be inserted in the current year, as stated. The Intercalation Remainder will also be useful in later calculations. In that con - nection, it should be noted that it can also be explained in connection with the sequence of Medial Qi, which begins each year with the Winter Solstice. At the start of a Rule, winter solstice coincides with the conjunction beginning the Celestial First Month. This condition recurs at the beginning of the next Rule 19 years later, but the conjunction with which the first winter solstice of that Rule coincides is seven later than the one that would have been indicated if winter solstices were separated by exactly 12 lunations each. So each successive winter solstice is 7/19 of a lunation later than its predecessor with respect to its Celestial First Month conjunction, and it is the total of this lag that is represented by Intercalation Remainder.

chunks.heading: 3.2.4 [Pr ocedures for sun and moon]
chunks.text:
推天正朔日， 置入蔀積月， 以蔀日乘之， 滿蔀月得一， 名為積日， 不滿為小餘， 積日以六十 除去之， 其餘為大餘， 以所入蔀名命之， 筭盡之外， 則前年天正十一月朔日 也． 小餘四百四十一以上， 其月大． 求後月朔， 加大餘二十九， 小餘四百九十 [九]， 小餘滿蔀月得一， 上加大餘， 命之如前．

§47 Set out the Accumulated Months into the Obscuration. Multiply by Obscura - tion Days [27,759]. Count one for each Obscuration Months [940] filled. Call that Accumulated Days. The remainder is the Lesser Remainder. Cast out 60 from the Accumulated Days. The remainder is the Greater Remainder. Count off from the [sexagenary] name of the Obscuration, and outside the exhausted count will be the day of Celestial Standard Conjunction in the eleventh [civil] month preceding the [civil] year. If the Lesser Remainder is 441 or greater, the month is long. To find the conjunction day of the next month, add 29 to the Greater Remainder, and 499 to the Lesser Remainder. Count one each time the Lesser Remainder fills Obscuration Months [940]. Take that unit up to the Greater Remainder. Count off as before. We now use the previous result to find the actual day of the Celestial Standard Conjunction, which begins the first Celestial month. First we convert the Accu- mulated Months into days by using the fact that 27,759 days are precisely equal to 940 months. The whole days resulting from this procedure tell us how many whole days have elapsed from the midnight commencing the current Obscuration up to midnight beginning the current year. Since we are interested in sexagenary day names, we can usefully cast out 60 from this amount to form the Greater Remainder as specified in order to find the sexagenary day name of the first day of the current year. To take an example: if we are in the second year of the Obscuration, Accumulated Months will be 12. Since: 12 × 27,759/940 = 354 remainder 348 and 354 mod 60 = 54 the Greater Remainder is 54, so the sexagenary day name of the first day of this year will be 54 further on than the sexagenary day name of the first day of the Obscura- tion. Note that the text does not treat this as a simple addition – we are to start counting from 1 to 54, starting at the sexagenary day name of the first day of the Obscuration, and then the day name after we finish (‘exhaust’) the count will be the one required. It is assumed but not stated that if the sexagenary day name passes 60 we shall start again at 1. In our example, the Lesser Remainder 348 is the fraction of a day at a scale of Obscuration Months [940] left when months are converted to days. It rep - resents the fraction of a day after midnight when the mean conjunction falls. Now, since 27,759/940 = 29 + 499/940, the Greater Remainder will increase by 29 each month, and the Lesser Remainder by 499, as stated. If the Lesser Remainder at the start of the month is already at least 940 − 499 = 441, then clearly the mean conjunction will fall at least a whole day after midnight at the start of the next month, and we shall have to wait 30 rather than 29 days for that month to begin, so that the current month is long, rather than a short 29 days. 一術，

chunks.heading: 3.2.4 [Pr ocedures for sun and moon]
chunks.text:
以大周乘年， 周天乘[閏餘]減之， 餘滿蔀(日)[月]， 則天正朔日也．

§48 Multiply the years by Greater Circuits [343,335]. Diminish it by Circuits of Heaven [1461] multiplied by Intercalation Remainder. As for the remain- der, [find] the amount of filled Obscuration Months [940]. Then that is the day of the Celestial Standard Conjunction. Greater Circuits [343,335] is the number of days in a solar cycle (i.e. winter solstice to winter solstice) at a scale of Obscuration Months [940]. Thus the first multiplica- tion gives the number of days elapsed from the start of the Obscuration up to the current winter solstice at a scale of 940. Now the Intercalation Remainder as already noted is the amount by which the start of the new year is in advance of its ideal date, which should coincide with winter solstice. It is in months, at a scale of Rule Factor [19]. We need to convert this to days and change the scale to 940 to make this compatible with the previ- ous result. As explained above, this can be done by multiplying by Circuits of Heaven [1461]. Subtracting the second result from the first and dividing by 940 therefore gives the number of days from the start of the Obscuration up to the first day of the first Celestial month of the current year, and the sexagenary day name of the day in question can easily be found by methods already described.

chunks.heading: 3.2.4 [Pr ocedures for sun and moon]
chunks.text:
推二十四氣 術曰：置入蔀年減一， 以(月)[日]餘乘之， 滿中法得一， 名曰大餘， 不滿為 小餘， 大餘滿六十除去之， 其餘以蔀名命之， 筭盡之外， 則前年冬至之日也. 求次氣， 加大餘十五， 小餘七， 除命之如前， 小寒日也．

§49 Method: set out the years entered into the Obscuration and subtract one. Multiply by the Day Remainder [168]. Count one for each Medial [Qi] factor [32] filled. Call that the Greater Remainder. What does not fill [a Medial [Qi] factor [32]] is the Lesser Remainder. Cast out mul - tiples of sixty from the Greater Remainder. With what is left, count off from the Obscuration name, then outside the exhausted count, that is the day of the winter solstice preceding this year. To predict the location of the next qi, add fifteen to the Greater Remainder, to the Lesser Remain - der 7, cast out and count off as before, and that is the day of Lesser Cold. The Day Remainder [168] is the extra days in the annual cycle of qi when multiples of 60 have been cast out, at a scale of Medial [Qi] factor [32], so for each year after the start of the Obscuration we have to add this amount to the day number of the initial day of the Obscuration (which is a winter solstice) to find the sexa - genary day name of the winter solstice preceding the start of the current civil year. The Lesser Remainder is the fraction of a day that the qi begins after midnight, at a scale of Medial [ Qi] factor [32]. Note that once again we subtract one from the ordinal number of an event in a series to find the interval from the start of the first event in a series to the start of this event.

chunks.heading: 3.2.4 [Pr ocedures for sun and moon]
chunks.text:
推閏月所在， 以閏餘減章法， 餘以十二乘之， 滿章閏數得一， 滿四以上亦得一筭之數， 從前 年十一月起， 筭盡之外， 閏月也． 或進退， 以中氣定之．

§50 Subtract the Intercalation Remainder from Rule Factor [19]. Multiply the remainder by 12. Count one for each completed Rule Intercalation Number [7]; for a completed four also get one count. Start from the eleventh month preceding this year; the month outside the exhausted count is the intercalary month. [Thus] there may be adjustments back and forth, and these are determined by [the position of] the Medial qi. In Proc. 3.5, it was determined whether the current year contains an intercalary month. If there is an intercalary month, this procedure finds where it will come in the sequence of months. The key to making this decision is to look for a luna - tion within which no medial qi is located. That lunation normally corresponds to an intercalary month – with, as we shall see, a slight adjustment to allow for certain borderline conditions. We begin by finding Intercalation Remainder, the remainder from: (Years into Obscuration) × 235/19. The whole number result of this division is the total number of whole mean lunations elapsed from the start of the current Obscuration up to the conjunc - tion which began the current (Celestial) year, which will include some lunations corresponding to intercalations in previous years. The remainder represents the amount in (1/19) of a mean lunation by which the winter solstice near the beginning of this year lags behind the conjunction of the first Celestial month, and this increases by (7/19) of a lunation from one winter solstice to the next. Now there are 12 medial qi in a year. So the lag between a medial qi and its preceding conjunction must increase steadily from medial qi to medial qi by (7/19) / (12) = 7/228 of a mean lunation. Since we are counting up the increasing lag in units of (1/228) of a mean lunation, and the Intercalation Remainder is in (1/19) of a lunation, it is clear that the initial multiplication by 12 is needed to convert the Intercalation Remainder to the correct scale, since 12 × 19 = 228. When the total lag for a given medial qi builds up to greater than 228/228 of a mean lunation, then that medial qi falls after the next mean conjunction, and the lunation preceding that medial qi contains no medial qi at all, since the previous medial qi fell just before the previous mean conjunction. The month corresponding to that lunation is therefore counted as intercalary; it bears the same number as the preceding month, with the prefix run 閏 ‘intercalary’. We then find how many times we need to add 7 to the scaled up Intercalation Remainder until we reach a total exceeding 228. Having found this number, then if we start counting with winter solstice taken as #1, and if (say) 3 additions of 7 are required to reach 228, the 4th qi will be the one ‘outside the count’ that has shifted onto or past the next mean conjunction. Suppose for example that the Intercalation Remainder is 14 for this year. That means the winter solstice lagged 14/19 of a lunation behind the Celestial First Month conjunction. In order for an intercalation to occur, we therefore need the remainder to increase by 19 − 14 = 5 We multiply by 12 to obtain 60, thus converting the scale from 19 to 228, and then count off sevens from this, each seven representing a medial qi past winter solstice that must pass before an intercalation is triggered. Now 60/7 = 8, remainder 4 So it will take 9 more medial qi after winter solstice, the first medial qi, before we accumulate the required remainder of 228. Thus it will be the 10th medial qi that will lag its corresponding (10th) conjunction by enough to take it past the next (11th) conjunction. The 10th lunation therefore contains no medial qi. It will thus be counted as the lunation of the intercalary 9th month, and it is the next lunation that will contain the 10th medial qi and thus correspond to the 10th month of the Celestial count. Of course the intercalary 9th Celestial month is the intercalary 7th civil month; we reach that number if we start counting from the 11th civil month of the preceding year, rather than the first Celestial month. What is the point of the statement that we should count a month ‘for each completed four’? This relates to a practice that we have already noted in the period when the Triple Concordance was in use – although as we have seen there is no explicit description in the system itself. The practice was that if the medial qi falls so near the next conjunction that it actually falls within the same day as that conjunction, then it is counted as falling within the next lunation. As a result, an intercalary month will be counted one month earlier than would otherwise have been the case. The ‘completed four’ method gives us a rough and ready way of telling when this shift might be called for. We may note that: 4/228 of a lunation is (4/228) × (29 499/940) days = 478/940 days to 3 significant figures, just over half a day. So the ‘completed four’ method places the qi in the next lunation if that qi falls within half a day before the conjunction, so that the current lunation corresponds to an intercalary month. If the interval is larger than 4/228 but less than 7/228 day, the next month will be intercalary.

chunks.heading: 3.2.4 [Pr ocedures for sun and moon]
chunks.text:
推弦、望日， 因其月朔大小餘之數， 皆加大餘七， 小餘三百五十九四分三， 小餘滿蔀月 得一， 加大餘， 大餘命如法， 得上弦． 又加得望， 次下弦， 又後月朔． 其弦、望 小餘二百六十以下， 每以百刻乘之， 滿蔀月得一刻， 不滿其(數)[所]近節氣 夜漏之半者， 以筭上為日．

§51 T ake the numbers for the Greater and Lesser Remainders for this month, and in each case add to the Greater Remainder 7 and the Lesser Remainder 359¾. Count one if the Lesser Remainder fills Obscuration Months [940], and add that to the Greater Remainder. Count off the Greater Remainder according to the method, and that is the [sexagenary day name] of the first crescent. A further addition gives full moon, the next gives the last crescent, and again after that the next conjunction. If the Lesser Remainders for crescents and full moon are 260 or less, in each case multiply by 100 ke, and count one ke for each filling of Obscuration Months [940]. Where this does not fill half the night clepsydra run for the nearest Nodal qi, then count one back to find the day [in whose night this event occurs]. The length of the mean lunation is (29 + 499/940) days, defined by: [Obscuration Days [27,759]]/[Obscuration Months [940]] Taking a quarter of this, we obtain: (7 + (359 + ¾) / 940) days for the interval between the events considered here. Hence the additions specified to the Greater and Lesser Remainders, with allow - ance for a whole extr a day mounting up as the factor of 940 is filled. The final section deals with the timing of the phase during the day. It seems, however, that specialists in li did not naturally think of their timings as starting from midnight, but preferred to think how much of the night was past, starting from dusk (when the night clepsydra was started) and running to dawn (when the day clepsydra was started). The night lengths given later for the principal seasons (see Table 3.11) are summarised in Table 3.3. The Lesser Remainders correspond to half the night length, 940 representing a whole day and night:

[TABLE_3_3] From this it is clear that the figure of 260 is a rounded value for the time from mid- night to dawn at the equinoxes in Lesser Remainder terms, designed to indicate roughly whether the phase is occurring during the hours of darkness at the start of the day. It is unclear why we are not told how to tell whether the phase falls after dusk on a given day, but that would be easy enough to deal with if required. From the final statement, it is evident that the whole of a given night was reckoned as belonging for astronomical (and hence divinatory) purposes to the day in which it began. Hence (in modern terms) an event at 2:00 am on Tuesday would be reckoned as having taken place during the night of Monday.

chunks.heading: 3.2.4 [Pr ocedures for sun and moon]
chunks.text:
推沒滅術， 置入蔀年減一， 以沒數乘之， 滿日法得一， 名為積沒， 不盡為沒餘． 以通法乘 積沒， 滿沒法得一， 名為大餘， 不盡為小餘． 大餘滿六十除去之， 其餘以蔀名 命之， 筭盡之外， 前年冬至前沒日也． 求後沒， 加大餘六十九， 小餘四， 小餘滿 沒法， 從大餘， 命之如前， 無分為滅．

§52 Set out years of entry into the Obscuration and subtract one. Multiply by Extinction Number [21], and obtain one for each filling of the Day Factor [4]. Called this Accumulated Extinctions. What is not exhausted is Extinction Remainder. Multiply Accumulated Extinctions by Compat - ibility Factor [487], and count one for each filling of Extinction Factor [7]. Call this the Greater Remainder. What is not exhausted is the Lesser Remainder. As the Greater Remainder fills 60, cast it out, and count off the remainder from the Obscuration [sexagenary day] name. Outside the exhausted count, that is the Extinction Day before the winter solstice of the preceding [civil] year. To predict the next Extinction, add 69 to the Greater Remainder, and 4 to the Lesser Remainder, and as the Lesser Remainder fills the Extinction Factor [7], let that go with the Greater Remainder, and count off as before. When there are no fractions, that is Obliteration. Since the interval from one winter solstice to the next is 1461/4 days, and this is equal to 360 + 5¼ = 360 + 21/4 days winter solstices do not all occur on the same sexagenary day. It would however be very convenient if they did. To deal with this problem, we do something akin to intercalation, by considering a ‘basic’ solar cycle of 360 days, in which all qi are assumed to fall on the same cyclical day as the preceding year. We then allow for the fact that extra days do in fact accumulate at the rate of 21/4 per solar cycle, so that the cyclical days on which qi fall shift further through the sexage - nary sequence. The total number of whole extra days accumulated to date is the Accumulated Extinctions. The question then arises as to when precisely the extra days amounted to the whole number which is Accumulated Extinctions: that day is the Extinction Day. Now the number of days in the year is 1461/4, and each year accumulates an extra 21/4 days. So each day in the year contributes: (21/4) / (1461/4) days = 7/487 days (So NB that each of the 24 qi contributes (21/4) / 24 = 7/32 days. Thus each whole day of a qi may be taken as contributing 7 / (15 × 32) days) 487 is the Compatibility Factor and 7 is the Extinction Factor, as indicated. Alternatively, we may say that each day of Extinction takes 487/7 = 69 + 4/7 days Hence multiplying Accumulated Extinctions by 487 and dividing by 7 gives us the number of days from the start of the current Obscuration to the moment of Extinction. Since 487/7 = 69, remainder 4, adding these numbers as specified will take us to the next Extinction Day. If on any given Extinction Day there is no fractional remainder, that is an Obliteration. 一術，

chunks.heading: 3.2.4 [Pr ocedures for sun and moon]
chunks.text:
以(為)[十]五乘冬至小餘， 以減通法， 餘滿沒法得一， 則天正後沒也．

§53 Multiply the Lesser Remainder of the winter solstice by 15, and subtract from Compatibility Factor [487]. Obtain 1 as the remainder fills Extinction Factor [7], then that is the Extinction after the Celestial Standard [conjunction]. The Lesser Remainder of the winter solstice is the remainder when years into the Obscuration are multiplied by Day Remainder [168] and divided by Medial [ Qi] factor [32]. It takes on the values 0,8,16 and 24 over a four-year cycle. Since one year contributes 21/4 days towards an Extinction, each of the 24 qi contributes (21/4) / 24 = 7/32 days. So . . . each of the 15 days of a qi may be taken as contributing 7 / (15 × 32) days). So if we have a Lesser Remainder at the usual scale of 32, that has taken [Lesser Remainder] × 15/7 days to accumulate, and that is the time since the last Extinc - tion. Thus, since Extinctions are 487/7 days apart, the time to the next Extinction is (487 − 15 × [Lesser Remainder]) / 7 days – as specified. Checking in detail: The gaps from the previous Extinction to the winter solstice commencing the second year of the Obscuration is: 365 − 5 × 487/7 since there were five Extinctions before the winter solstice = 5 × (73 − 487/7) = 5 × (511 − 487) / 7 = 5 × (24/7) = 15 × (8/7) So the next year the gap will be twice this, at 15 × (16/7) And in the next year the gap will be: 15 × (24/7) And these gaps are in each case (Lesser Remainder for winter solstice) × 15/7. Clearly therefore we can find the gap from winter solstice to the subsequent extinction by subtracting these amounts from 487/7 as specified.

chunks.heading: 3.2.4 [Pr ocedures for sun and moon]
chunks.text:
推合朔所在度， 置入蔀積月以[蔀]日乘之， 滿大周除去之， 其餘滿蔀月得一， 名為積度， 不盡為餘分． 積度加斗二十一度， 加二百三十五分， 以宿次除之, 不滿宿， 則日月合朔所在 (星)[宿] 度也． 求後合朔， 加度二十九， 加分四百九 十九， 分滿蔀月得一度， 經斗除二百三十五分．

§54 Set out the Accumulated Months of entry into the Obscuration, multiply by Obscuration days [27,759], and cast out and discard what fills Greater Circuits [343,335]. As for the remainder, obtain 1 for each filling of Obscu- ration Months [940]. Call this Accumulated Du. What is not exhausted is Remainder Parts. To the Accumulated Du, add the 21 du of Dipper, with [its] 235 parts, and then for each Lodge cast out in succession. When it does not fill a Lodge, then that is the du of the Lodge 13 at which the sun and moon are located at their conjunction. To seek the next conjunction, add to the du 29, and add to the Parts 499, obtaining 1 du as the Parts fill Obscuration Months [940], and casting out 235 Parts as you pass through Dipper. Accumulated Months have already been calculated for the conjunction of the first Celestial (and hence subsequent) months in Proc. 3.6. Obscuration Days [27,759] is the number of days in a month at a scale of Obscuration Months [940], so the multiplication specified produces the number of days elapsed at the instant of conjunction (and hence number of du moved by the sun), including fractional parts, at a scale of Obscuration Months [940]. Greater Circuits [343,335] = 365¼ × 940, so this represents the du in a complete circuit at the same scale. Casting this out gives the number of du moved by the sun past its starting point at winter solstice – which is also the du moved by the moon at the time of the conjunction, since its position coincides with that of the sun. If we want to locate the present position of the sun and moon in the lodge system, then we have to take account of the fact that in the system used by the Han Quarter Remainder, winter solstice position of the sun is at 21¼ du of the lodge Dipper. Thus to count movement of the sun from the start of Dipper we have to add this amount, with the ¼ du in the form 235/940. We then move through the lodge system casting out the different extensions of each lodge in turn until we find which lodge the sun is located in at the time of the conjunc - tion. As the text notes, when we pass through Dipper again (which is in all 26 235/940 du across) we must remember to deduct the fraction as well as the whole du of this lodge. Since the length of a mean lunation is 29 499/940 days, this is also the number of du that the sun moves between conjunctions. By adding this amount we can move from the position just calculated to the next conjunction position. The received text runs 置入蔀積月以日乘之 ‘Set out the Accumulated Months of entry into the Obscuration, multiply by days’ which is clearly defective. I emend following the version of Li Rui, which involves only the insertion of 蔀 ‘Obscuration’ before ‘days’, and produces an exact result for the position of moon and sun at the moment of conjunction: see (Li Rui 李銳 (1768–1817) 1993: 760B). The editors of the Zhonghua edition adopt a more complex emendation, in accordance with the views of Qian Daxin 置入蔀積(月)[日]以(日)[蔀月]乘之 ‘Set out the Accumulated Days of entry into the Obscuration, and multiply by Obscu- ration Months [940]’ : see Hou Han shu, zhi 3, 3063. However, this only produces the position of the moon and sun on the midnight of the day on which the conjunction falls, not at the moment of conjunction itself. Li Rui’s simpler read - ing is clearly preferable. 一術，

chunks.heading: 3.2.4 [Pr ocedures for sun and moon]
chunks.text:
以閏餘乘周天， 以減大周餘， 滿蔀月得一， 合以斗二十一度四分一， 則天正合 朔日月所在度．

§55 Multiply Circuits of Heaven [1461] by Intercalation Remainder, and by that subtract from Greater Circuits [343,335], obtaining 1 as the remainder fills Obscuration Months [940]. Join with it the 21 du ¼ of Dipper, and this is the du where the sun and moon are located at the Celestial Standard conjunction. Intercalation Remainder is the fraction of a month at a scale of 19 by which the conjunction of Celestial New Year falls in advance of the winter solstice. Now the days in a lunation (and hence the du moved by the sun between conjunctions) are given by: 19 × Circuits of Heaven [1461]/Obscuration Months [940]. Since as before the number of du in a whole circuit is represented by Greater Circuits [343,335]/Obscuration Months [940], the procedure described here moves us backwards from the sun’s winter solstice position to its location at the preceding conjunction, as required.

chunks.heading: 3.2.4 [Pr ocedures for sun and moon]
chunks.text:
推日所在度， 置入蔀積日之數， 以蔀法乘之， 滿蔀日除去之， 其餘滿蔀法得一， 為積 度， 不盡為餘分． 積度加斗二十一度， 加十九分， 以宿次除去之， 則夜半日所 在宿度也． 求次日， 加一度． 求次月， 大加三十度， 小加二十九度， 經斗除十

[九]分． §56 Set out the number of Accumulated Days entered into the Obscuration, and multiply it by Obscuration Factor [76]. Cast out and discard Obscuration Days [27,759], and obtain 1 for each time the remainder fills Obscuration Factor [76], which is Accumulated Du, while what is not exhausted is Remainder Parts. To the Accumulated Du add the 21 du of Dipper and add 19 parts, then cast out and discard the Lodges in sequence, and that is the degree of the Lodges where the sun is located at midnight. To seek the next day, add 1 du. To seek the next month, add 30 du for a long [month] and 29 du for a short [month]. When passing through Dipper cast out the 19 parts. At the beginning of an Obscuration cycle, the sun is at winter solstice. Each day thereafter it moves 1 du. Since the days in a solar cycle, and hence the du moved in that cycle, are given by: Obscuration Days [27,759]/Obscuration Factor [76] = 365¼, The procedure given yields the du from winter solstice moved by the sun in the current cycle, and the rest follows. ‘19 parts’ here are 19/76 = ¼. 一術，

chunks.heading: 3.2.4 [Pr ocedures for sun and moon]
chunks.text:
以朔小餘減合[朔]度分， 即日夜半所在． 其分(三)[二]百(二)[三]十五約之, 十九乘之．

§57 By the Lesser Remainder for the conjunction subtract from the du and parts for the conjunction, then that is where the sun is located at midnight. As for the parts simplify them by 235, multiplying by 19. The Lesser Remainder is the fraction of a day, at the scale of Obscuration Months [940] by which the conjunction falls after midnight, and hence it gives the angular movement of the sun between these instants. It will be recalled that the factor giving the scale of Parts in the calculation of the sun’s midnight position was 76. To convert to this from a scale of 940 requires a multiplication of the parts by 235/19, as specified.
